Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE:TSM) has surged 13.14% over the last six months, as of October 15. This compares to a 21.5% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 15.74% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. TSMC just had a strong third quarter, with revenue rising 41.2% from a year earlier to $46.7 billion. Net income grew even faster, jumping 68.7%. AI-related chips are driving much of this growth, with high-performance computing accounting for 68% of revenue. The company expects revenue to reach $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion in the fourth quarter and is now forecasting full-year revenue growth of around 44%. What's interesting is that demand isn't coming only from AI accelerators. TSMC is also seeing more demand for CPUs used in AI servers and networking chips. As companies move from chatbots toward AI assistants that can carry out tasks, they may need more computing power. TSMC's CEO said demand for leading-edge chips remains well above what the company can currently supply. The challenge is no longer just keeping up with demand for today's chips, but deciding how much capacity to build for the next few years. TSMC ranks 3rd in our list of 10 Best Stocks to Buy for the Next 20 Years. Click HERE to find out other stocks on the list. TSMC's advantage goes beyond having customers such as Nvidia and Apple. Manufacturing advanced chips at scale, with good yields and competitive costs, is extremely difficult. In the third quarter, technologies at 7 nanometers and below accounted for 79% of wafer revenue. Its 2nm process already contributed 8%, and management expects annual capacity for the N2 family to more than double in 2027. Advanced packaging is becoming just as important. As AI chips grow more complex, customers need ways to connect and package multiple components efficiently. TSMC is already producing large packages at good yields and working on even larger designs. This makes it harder for competitors to win business by matching one process technology alone. Customers need manufacturing capacity and packaging that work together, not just a promising chip design. TSM ranked 10th in our list of the 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE:TSM) plans to spend $60 billion to $64 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, with investment over 2026 to 2028 expected to be significantly higher than in the previous three years. It has also committed another $100 billion to US expansion, bringing its planned US investment to $265 billion, and is evaluating further capacity in Texas. These projects bring production closer to customers, but they are expensive. The cost is already showing up in margins. Gross margin fell from 67.7% in the second quarter to 66.4% in the third, mainly because of the 2nm ramp. Overseas factories will add further pressure, with management expecting them to reduce gross margin by 3 to 4 percentage points in the latter part of the coming five-year period. TSMC believes revenue growth will outpace capital spending, but that still needs to play out. The company has also warned that price-sensitive consumer markets are under pressure, so not every part of its business is enjoying the AI boom. TSM ranked first in our list of the Top 10 AI Stocks to Buy According to Billionaire Philippe Laffont. To see which other stocks made the list, click HERE. TSMC is trading at 33.67x its trailing earnings and 21.41x its future earnings. The difference indicates that analysts expect the company's profits to increase considerably in the coming year. That by itself does not mean the stock is cheap. However, considering the near-monopolistic characteristic of the company, those multiples seem reasonable. There is a good reason for those expectations. Third-quarter net income grew nearly 69% year over year. At 21.41x forward earnings, TSMC doesn't look unreasonable for a business growing this quickly, especially with a 51.1% net margin in the latest quarter. Its manufacturing lead gives it a way to benefit from AI spending. But investors have to look beyond the next few quarters. TSMC's stock weakened even after its latest record results, as the wider chip selloff raised questions about the returns on massive AI infrastructure spending. If customers slow their investment before the new factories reach full production, TSMC could face lower capacity utilization just as its costs rise. That would put pressure on both earnings estimates and the valuation, which would be a double whammy for the stock. The stock's appeal depends on more than strong demand today. It depends on that demand lasting long enough to justify the investments being made now. TSM ranked 18th in our list of the 20 Best Performing Stocks Over the Last 20 Years. To see which stocks outranked it, click HERE. TSMC is in a good position to gain from AI over the coming several years, and its strengths in manufacturing and packaging are hard to copy. Although the stock looks a great long-term buy, it isn't a low-hanging fruit anymore. The main point is whether earnings can continue to grow fast enough to make the massive investment in new capacity worthwhile. So far, the figures back up the argument. It will be in the coming years that we will see if TSMC can keep delivering those returns as the business increases in size and becomes more costly to operate. June sales rose 37% to NT$401.26 billion. The company will release its full results and outlook on Thursday. TSMC makes cutting-edge semiconductors for the likes of Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and components for Apple. The biggest buyers of those chips – including cloud companies Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft – have set aside $725 billion for AI-related investments this year. The latest performance shows steady demand for advanced chips, which power data centers and other systems that power AI applications, smartphones and automobiles. In April, the Taiwanese giant raised its full-year sales guidance and said its capital spending should trend toward the upper end of an existing forecast range of up to $56 billion in 2026. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced in May that the U.S. chip designer would set up a headquarters in Taiwan and invest up to $150 billion annually in the region. Still, TSMC CEO C.C. Wei had warned in June that his company won’t be able to meet demand from American customers for years, even as more manufacturing capacity comes online in the U.S. over the next few years. The campaign comes as investors search for Hims’ next major growth engine beyond compounded GLP-1 drugs, and as regulators prepare to decide whether seven popular peptides should receive a clearer pathway into the U.S. compounding market. Hims said more than 170 peptides are in active clinical development, presenting the category as established science rather than a passing wellness trend. “Peptides aren’t new—they’ve been researched for decades,” the post said. “What’s changed? Former committee member Dr. Anita Gupta said earlier reviews raised “some red flags” over immunogenicity and pointed to reports of “heavy metals,” “microbial contamination” and mislabeling. It noted that BPC-157 has fewer than 36 human participants across three studies, KPV has no live-human trials and TB-500 has only one human tolerance study. The group also warned that compounding could falsely signal FDA approval and cited 127 peptide shipments entering U.S. ports in the first quarter, with about 39% coming from manufacturers outside FDA oversight. Shares of Circle (CRCL) were on track to hit a monthly high on pre-market trade on Friday following a dip to an over three-month low in the previous trading session. The uptick came after the company announced it had received final approval from the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to establish First National Digital Currency Bank. The final approval marks the end of a process that began in December 2025, when Circle first received conditional approval alongside Ripple (XRP), BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets, and Paxos. It will operate as Circle National Trust, a national trust bank that brings stablecoin USDC's (USDC) custody infrastructure under direct federal oversight. Shares of Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN) and Oracle Corp. (ORCL) were in focus on Friday after the U.K. government designated the four companies as Critical Third Parties (CTPs) to strengthen and safeguard the country’s financial systems. At the time of writing, MSFT stock was up 0.4%, ORCL shares climbed 1%, while GOOG and AMZN shares edged 0.2% lower each. The firms covered under the new framework are Microsoft Ireland Operations, Google Cloud EMEA, Amazon Web Services EMEA, and Oracle Corporation UK. Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will jointly oversee the critical services the four companies provide to the financial sector. The aim is to reduce the risk of widespread disruption if a major cloud provider experiences operational issues. Regulatory oversight will apply only to the financial sector, not to their broader business operations. The designated companies will be required to maintain strong systems to identify, manage, and recover from disruptions affecting services used by financial institutions. Regulators will also be allowed to gather information, assess operational resilience, and, when necessary, introduce or enforce CTP-specific rules to ensure the continuity of critical services. “These designations will help ensure the critical services financial firms rely on remain resilient, protecting consumers and businesses while supporting growth across the economy,” said Rachel Blake, Economic Secretary to the Treasury of the United Kingdom. The Critical Third Parties designation was established under the UK’s Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 to improve operational resilience after growing concerns that disruptions at major cloud providers could affect multiple financial institutions simultaneously. The framework builds on the Bank of England’s 2021 assessment that the financial sector’s increasing reliance on a small number of cloud providers warranted stronger regulatory oversight to safeguard essential financial services relied upon by millions of consumers and businesses. According to a CloudGuard Financial Services Threat Report published earlier this year, cyber risks faced by the U.K.’s financial sector have reached a record high, with the industry accounting for about 28% of all cyberattacks in the country. The report highlighted growing threats from ransomware, nation-state hackers, and AI-powered scams such as deepfakes and targeted phishing. It also warned of a sharp rise in credential theft, with billions of stolen login credentials circulating on the dark web. title: Soros Capital Loads Up On MU, AMAT, AMD And TSM In Massive Semiconductor Pivot - Stocktwits
content: Soros Capital Management LLC more than doubled its equity portfolio to $559 million in the second quarter of 2026, pivoting away from industrials and energy toward semiconductors and AI-related technology. The semiconductor sector has been one of the market’s strongest performers this year, fueled by booming demand for artificial intelligence and shortages of memory chips that have pushed prices higher. Major tech companies are also pouring huge sums into AI systems, further boosting the sector. The firm’s most notable moves were large new positions in chipmakers and related suppliers, according to its filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday for holdings as of June 30. Micron Technology (MU) debuted with a $42.5-million stake, making it the second-largest holding. Applied Materials (AMAT) followed with a $34.5-million new position, while Flex (FLEX) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) entered with $32.2 million and $30.2 million stakes, respectively. ON Semiconductor was also newly added at $20.6 million. The firm’s biggest single addition was the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY) at $42.8 million, giving broad exposure to Korean chip giants. Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) saw its position surge more than 1,300% to $37.5 million. Caterpillar (CAT) nearly doubled to $34.9 million. These changes pushed technology and semiconductor exposure to dominate the top of the book. To fund the shift, Soros Capital, which manages assets for the Soros family, sharply reduced or exited several industrial and energy names that had been prominent in the prior quarter. Comfort Systems USA (FIX) saw the largest cut, down $22.4 million. GE Vernova (GEV) was trimmed by $11.3 million, while Bloom Energy, Analog Devices (ADI), and Emcor Group (EME) were also significantly reduced or sold. Phillips 66 (PSX) and Marathon Petroleum (MPC) reportedly held merger talks earlier this year over a deal that would have created a $180 billion oil-and-gas giant. But the discussions ultimately fizzled out and are unlikely to be resurrected anytime soon, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Both PSX and MPC shares gained around 1% on Friday. At the time of writing on Friday midday, PSX stock was trading 0.15% higher, while MPC shares had pared all their gains and had edged down 0.05%. The talks taking place are a sign of the exuberance fueling mergers and acquisitions (M&A) under the Donald Trump administration, Semafor reported. A combination of Phillips 66 and Marathon Petroleum would have brought together businesses accounting for around a quarter of U.S. refining capacity and faced antitrust scrutiny, given there are only a handful of standalone refiners in the country. But administration officials have waved through a number of big mergers in other industries, including a $110-billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery and a $14-billion deal for Juniper Networks. Stanley Woodward, a top Justice Department official, has pushed to avoid trials in favor of settlements. A combined company would have been able to maintain a higher profit margin even when fuel prices dip, in part by negotiating stronger discounts from crude traders. The two companies also have a number of complementary businesses, including substantial pipeline and storage networks, although combining the operations would have been thorny. Phillips 66 has a joint venture with Chevron in chemicals, with each side having a right of first refusal to acquire the other side's wholly owned interest. Previous efforts by both Chevron and Phillips 66 to sell the business have reportedly run into hurdles. Marathon Petroleum also has a publicly traded but controlled subsidiary, MPLX, which would have added additional complexity to any combination. Future Fund managing partner Gary Black on Friday sharply shifted his view on a potential SpaceX (SPCX) acquisition of Tesla (TSLA), saying he now “fully expects” SpaceX to launch an all-equity offer at a healthy premium for Tesla sometime this year. “I fully expect $SPCX to make an all-equity offer at a healthy premium to acquire $TSLA sometime this year.  It makes Elon’s life easier, and there are clearly shared synergies,” Black wrote in a post on X. Just months earlier, Black dismissed the idea as highly unlikely. On May 22, he called a post-IPO merger “a very low probability event” with “no compelling business logic,” citing excessive dilution that would expand each firm’s market cap by 50% or more and a lack of clear synergies beyond Elon Musk’s control of both. In June and July posts, he reiterated that the “math won’t pass muster,” warned of fiduciary issues for SpaceX’s board, and labeled hopes of a buyout “greater fool theory.” His latest stance marks a clear reversal, driven by shared synergies and the deal’s potential to simplify Musk’s dual-CEO role. Black also predicts that many Tesla shareholders will sell on any announcement rather than wait 6-12 months for closing, citing intolerance of roughly 50% dilution and possible interim declines in the SpaceX shares received. Speculation about a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger has circulated for years, dating back well before SpaceX’s June 2026 IPO, as investors long noted the companies’ shared leadership under Elon Musk and overlapping ambitions in technology and manufacturing. The chatter intensified in early 2026 following SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI and reports that the rocket firm was weighing a combination with Tesla. After the IPO, the rumors surged further, centering on a possible all-stock deal to simplify Musk’s dual roles and capture synergies in AI, robotics, energy, and space. SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell addressed the speculation on the company’s June 12 IPO day. She told CNBC a combination “might make Elon’s life a little easier” and noted “no question that there are synergies between Tesla and SpaceX,” though she stressed her focus remains on operations. Tesla CEO Elon Musk, on the EV giant’s July 22 earnings call, pointed to “more and more overlap” from collaborations like the Terafab chip project but declined specifics, saying any combination must follow “the appropriate process.” On Friday, The Information also reported that Tesla is preparing to unveil a new design for its next-generation Roadster this month, which combines rocket technology from SpaceX for superior acceleration. The Walt Disney Co. (DIS) CEO Josh D’Amaro on Friday acknowledged investor frustration with the company’s stock price, but said the company is in a strong position as it enters its next chapter, pointing to its streaming business, theme parks, ESPN and movie slate. During an interview with CNBC on the sidelines of the D23 Expo, D’Amaro said that he is “feeling pretty good” about where Disney is right now, nearly six months into his role as the company’s CEO. “I'm not happy with where the stock stands right now. Our investors aren't happy with that, but I do believe that we're sitting in a very great space relative to the entertainment industry,” he said. Disney shares were up more than 1% in Friday morning’s trade. D’Amaro said Disney’s intellectual property gives the company an advantage as entertainment companies increasingly seek to acquire valuable franchises, scale and complementary businesses. “If you look at what’s happening all around us, companies are trying to acquire scale or acquire IP or acquire additional businesses. And the reason that they’re trying to do that is because they want to look a little bit more like Disney,” he added. D’Amaro pointed to Disney’s extensive library of characters and franchises as a key asset that can drive value across its businesses. “We have the deepest library of intellectual property and characters and franchises by far,” D’Amaro said. “Our scale is enviable. The connection that we have with fans, you see it here, right here at D23, is palpable.” D’Amaro said bringing those assets together under a unified Disney strategy could be particularly powerful for the company. “We have everything that we need right now, putting those things together, under, I got to put one Disney frame, I think, is exceptionally powerful,” he added. D’Amaro said Disney’s next chapter will focus on continuing growth in streaming, improving margins, investing in its experiences business, moving ESPN toward direct-to-consumer and delivering strong films. He pointed to the company’s recent performance as evidence that its strategy is already producing results. “It is not just me hoping, it’s gonna happen. We’re actually delivering on that,” D’Amaro said, referring to Disney’s streaming growth, parks performance and other businesses. He also said the company wants to move with “more speed and urgency,” embrace technology more aggressively, and operate as “one Disney.” D’Amaro said Disney’s opportunity lies in getting consumers to engage with multiple parts of its business, from theme parks and Disney+ to merchandise and movies. “One of the things we know is that if a consumer is exposed to multiple parts of our business, there is a theme park visitor that then becomes a Disney+ subscriber, that Disney+ subscriber, then buys merchandise,” he said. D’Amaro said consumers who interact with multiple Disney businesses generate significantly more value than those who engage with just one part of the company. Disney wants to make those interactions more seamless and bring its businesses together under a unified consumer experience. “If it’s a seamless fan experience, I think that lifetime value goes up, and we drive top line and bottom line,” D’Amaro said. He also pointed to Disney+ as a potential centerpiece for that strategy, saying the company wants to bring more of its businesses and experiences onto the streaming platform. Shares of Valneva (VALN) stock surged 24% on Friday after the European Medicines Agency accepted the marketing application for its experimental Lyme disease vaccine for review. Valneva developed the vaccine in partnership with Pfizer (PFE). If it receives regulatory approval, Pfizer will have exclusive rights to manufacture and commercialize it. VALN stock recorded its biggest single-day gains since June 2022, and is currently trading at its highest levels since March. PFE shares edged 0.2% lower. The validation means the application can now undergo a formal scientific assessment, a crucial step ahead of launch across the European Union. However, it does not indicate that the vaccine, known as PF-07307405, will ultimately be approved. Lyme disease is a bacterial infection that can cause rashes, joint aches, fatigue and nerve issues. PF-07307405 is the most advanced Lyme disease vaccine candidate, and no human vaccine has been approved to date, according to Pfizer. “Lyme disease remains the most common vector-borne illness in Europe, affecting more than 100,000 people each year. When left untreated, it can lead to serious and potentially long-lasting complications involving the skin, joints, nervous system, and heart,” said Annaliesa Anderson, Senior Vice President and Chief Vaccines Officer at Pfizer. The application is supported by the Phase 3 Valor trial completed earlier this year. The trial tested the vaccine in 9,437 people aged five and older across Lyme-endemic regions in the U.S., Canada and Europe. The vaccine was well tolerated, with no safety concerns identified during the analysis. However, the primary analysis failed to meet its predetermined statistical requirement because fewer Lyme disease cases occurred than expected. Pfizer has argued that the overall efficacy was clinically meaningful. ARK Investment Management, run by noted tech investor Cathie Wood, disclosed late Wednesday that it acquired $20 million of shares of TSMC. The stake was acquired by ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK), ARK Autonomous Technology & Robotics ETF (ARKQ), ARK Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW), and ARK Space Exploration & Innovation ETF (ARKX). Shares of the world’s biggest contract chip manufacturer have declined for six sessions straight until Wednesday, cumulatively losing 12% in this period. ARK has remained a long-term holder of TSM but has actively traded around the position, selling into rallies and adding on pullbacks. In 2026, however, ARK became a more opportunistic seller: it reduced its TSM stake by roughly 121,000 shares (16.1%) in the first quarter, sold about 100,500 additional shares worth approximately $40.6 million during the semiconductor rally in mid-May, and executed several smaller trims afterward as the stock approached record highs. The move comes after TSM reported upbeat results earlier this month. After posting second-quarter earnings that blew past market expectations, the Taiwanese firm raised its full-year revenue growth to slightly above 40% in dollar terms, up from its earlier estimate of above 30%. TSMC makes cutting-edge semiconductors for the likes of Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and components for Apple. The biggest buyers of those chips – including cloud companies Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft – have set aside $725 billion for AI-related investments this year. Currently, 34 out of 35 analysts recommend buying the stock, while a lone analyst rates the stock ‘Hold,’ per Koyfin data. Space stocks rose premarket on Thursday as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk reinforced confidence in Moon and Mars plans following bullish comments from NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman on the rocket firm’s role in America’s lunar ambitions. SPCX and RKLB edged up 0.1% in premarket trading, while ASTS gained 1%. Over the past month, however, all three have fallen sharply, with RKLB down 40%, ASTS off 39% and SPCX losing 31%. Musk said “It will happen” on X in response to a post from early SpaceX investor and X Prize Foundation Executive Chairman Peter Diamandis, who highlighted Isaacman’s conviction that Musk’s company will be instrumental in turning lunar ambitions into reality. Isaacman said: “If Elon and SpaceX are betting on this right now, there is no reason to believe this will not come into existence. I never bet against an extremely well-capitalized Elon.” He added that NASA’s top national space-policy objective is to return American astronauts to the lunar surface and build out a Moon base, saying of SpaceX: “We can’t do it without them.” NASA’s Artemis III mission, due in 2027, will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit to dock with prototype lunar landers rather than attempt a Moon landing. The mission was originally intended to return astronauts to the lunar surface, but NASA changed course in February after SpaceX’s Starship lander was not ready and its required in-orbit refueling technology had yet to be demonstrated. Artemis IV, targeted for 2028, is now scheduled to put Americans on the Moon for the first time since 1972. The longer-term ambition is a sustained human presence. NASA’s Moon Base program calls for robotic missions before 2029, repeated crewed missions from 2029 and semi-permanent habitats by the mid-2030s, with the Moon eventually serving as a proving ground for Mars exploration. SpaceX already holds multibillion-dollar Human Landing System awards covering an uncrewed lunar demonstration, crewed landings and later missions. A sustained Moon-base buildout would also mean more demand for high-capacity launches, cargo, infrastructure and landing systems, which are all central to the Starship strategy. The endorsement comes as SpaceX shares have pulled back from post-IPO highs amid valuation concerns, Starship execution questions and lockup-related supply worries, making NASA leadership’s backing an important sentiment catalyst. Rocket Lab stands to benefit more indirectly through increased launch and space-systems demand. The company already has lunar and planetary credentials through NASA’s Capstone mission and the twin Escapade spacecraft headed to Mars. Electron could benefit from more small science and infrastructure missions, while reusable medium-lift rocket Neutron, targeted for a first flight later in 2026, could compete for larger constellation, logistics and dedicated missions. While AST SpaceMobile has limited direct Moon or Mars exposure, it could benefit from stronger investor appetite for commercial-space stocks. ASTS relies heavily on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 for BlueBird deployments as it ramps its constellation toward 45 satellites for initial continuous coverage in key markets. The company also has U.S. government awards for tactical and resilient communications, giving it another potential avenue as national space investment expands. Retail traders favor SPCX right now. Shares of Viking Therapeutics, Inc. (VKTX) have been July’s biggest laggard among weight-loss stocks, but CEO Brian Lian says the company’s lead obesity drug could stand out by giving patients multiple treatment options, including a weekly shot, a daily pill and potentially less-frequent dosing to help keep weight off. VKTX stock fell 1% on Wednesday, extending its weekly decline to 4% and putting the shares on track for a third consecutive week of losses. Over the past month, VKTX has fallen 15%, compared with declines of 8% for Structure Therapeutics (GPCR), 2% for Eli Lilly (LLY) and 1% for Altimmune (ALT), while Novo Nordisk (NVO), Amgen (AMGN), Terns Pharmaceuticals (TERN) and Regeneron (REGN) have posted gains. Late Wednesday, Viking posted a loss of $1.10 per share for the second quarter (Q2), better than the $1.15 loss analysts had expected, but wider than the $0.58 loss a year earlier. The company remains pre-revenue, making clinical progress the key focus for investors. Viking’s lead obesity drug, VK2735, is being developed as both a weekly injection and a daily pill. Its two Phase 3 Vanquish trials of the injectable version are fully enrolled and advancing according to plan, while two Phase 3 studies of the oral version are expected to begin in the fourth quarter. Lian said Viking believes the oral version could become the first dual GLP-1/GIP agonist pill to reach the market. The company is also testing whether patients can maintain weight loss with injections given every other week or once a month. Results from that study are due later this quarter. Lian said on the company’s latest earnings call: “We will have, if we're successful, a product that is very effective on a weekly basis. We think probably very effective on an oral basis, then potentially very effective with a reduced dosing frequency sort of option, and no one else has that.” He also called VK2735’s profile “really competitive” and “differentiated from other advanced programs.” In Phase 2, injectable VK2735 delivered up to 15% average weight loss after 13 weekly doses with “no signs of plateau,” while the oral version produced up to 12% average weight loss over 13 weeks. Up to 80% of oral-treated patients lost at least 10% of their body weight, versus 5% on placebo, and Viking said gastrointestinal side effects at planned doses were not meaningfully different from placebo. Viking is now testing whether patients can maintain weight loss with weekly, every-other-week or monthly dosing after initial treatment. Management hopes to identify two to four regimens for further study and believes retaining about 75% to 80% of initial weight loss could preserve long-term health benefits. Oral maintenance regimens are also planned, with that portion expected to wrap up in the first half of 2027. Viking has also started Phase 1 testing of VK3019, a separate experimental obesity drug targeting amylin and calcitonin receptors. Preclinical studies showed up to 8% weight reduction versus controls after a single dose. Lian said adding an amylin drug to a GLP-1 treatment has typically improved efficacy by 40% to 50%, and a similar boost on top of VK2735 could deliver an “industry-leading level of efficacy.” A combination program would not enter clinical testing until 2027 at the earliest. title: TSMC CEO Hints Company Could Step In If Intel Cannot Meet Customers’ Advanced Packaging Demand - Stocktwits
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) CEO C.C. Wei hinted during the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker could step in if customers struggle to secure enough advanced-packaging supply from Intel (INTC). The remarks came after Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan asked whether TSMC would support customers that initially chose Intel’s EMIB-T packaging technology but later faced supply constraints, according to the Koyfin transcript of the company’s third-quarter (Q3) earnings call. “I try to avoid answering it directly, but let me say that, yes, we will be,” Wei said. “Number one priority I already indicated is that TSMC’s customer’s product can be introduced into the market smoothly. That’s a number one priority. Okay? And that gives you enough of a hint.” TSM stock fell nearly 4% in morning trade amid broader market weakness as concerns around AI spending and hotter-than-expected producer prices weighed on markets. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment behind the chip supplier to companies like Nvidia (NVDA) and Apple (AAPL), improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Platform data showed a 666% increase in chatter in the same time period. Intel’s EMIB-T and TSMC’s Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) are competing approaches to advanced packaging that connect chip components and high-bandwidth memory into integrated systems used in AI computing. A shortage of packaging capacity can delay deliveries even when the underlying chips are available. Should that happen, clients can either delay their launch or switch to a different supplier. During Intel’s second-quarter (Q2) earnings call in July, CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated that  EMIB-T orders were growing and yield and reliability targets were being met, with the company preparing to scale production to support customers’ 2027 ramps. INTC stock fell over 5% in morning trade on Thursday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the company continued to trend in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day. Wei said TSMC is already producing packages five times the standard reticle size, with plans to expand to nine times and eventually 14 times that size. “We are in the real-world production of 5x reticle size. I don’t believe that anybody can do that today except at TSMC, and the yield is excellent,” he said. “So our customers are very satisfied with the result.” Wei added that the company is also working to reduce packaging costs, stating that its CoWoS technology remains customers’ preferred option. TSM stock fell in morning trade on Thursday despite reporting a Q3 earnings and revenue beat. Earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.91, according to Koyfin, beating Wall Street expectations of $0.89 per share. Apollo Global Management (APO) Chief Economist Torsten Slok stated that the Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy choice as producer prices accelerate and consumers begin pulling back on spending, raising the risk of an uncomfortable mix of persistent inflation and slowing economic growth. “This is a definition of stagflation,” Slok said during a CNBC interview. “We have higher prices, and in response to higher prices, we buy less.” His comments came after U.S. producer price inflation accelerated sharply in August, defying expectations for a decline. The annual producer price index (PPI) rose to 6.3%, its second-highest level in four years, higher than the expected 5.5%. Monthly headline PPI climbed 1.3%, more than double the 0.6% increase economists had expected. Core PPI also exceeded expectations, with the monthly reading coming in at 0.7% against an estimate of 0.3%. U.S. equities traded lower ahead of the PPI data release. After markets opened, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were on track to hit their worst week since June. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.4%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 1.3%. According to Slok, the hotter inflation reading complicates the Fed’s efforts to balance price stability against the risk of slowing growth. Slok said policymakers must decide whether to prioritize rising inflation or signs that consumers are beginning to rein in spending. “The challenge for the Fed is: Should they be focusing on inflation going up, or should they be focusing on the slowdown in consumers’ money and the risk of GDP growth?” he said. Slok pointed to housing and autos as early examples of interest-rate-sensitive sectors responding to tighter financial conditions. Mortgage rates have climbed substantially from their pandemic-era lows, while financing and leasing a car have become more expensive. “The more interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy are beginning to respond,” Slok said. “We’re seeing that in housing. We’re seeing that in autos.” He added that consumers are also showing early signs of adjusting their spending as higher prices squeeze household budgets. Slok also warned that the U.S. economy has become increasingly dependent on AI investment, leaving growth vulnerable if companies slow spending on data centers and related infrastructure. “GDP growth is normally two [percent], and now roughly one percentage point of GDP is coming from the AI spending boom,” he said. A slowdown in the build-out could weigh on economic growth even without triggering a recession. The key question, Slok said, is whether the financial returns from AI investment arrive as quickly as investors expect. “What if that payoff does not arrive with the speed that the consensus was expecting?” he said. Slok expects some moderation in data center construction as expectations for earnings and investment returns adjust, but does not anticipate a recession. “I think the answer is that we will not get a recession, but I do think we’ll get some more dampening of the data center build-out,” he said. With PPI inflation at its second-highest level in four years, CME FedWatch data put the odds of a Fed rate hike at 27.1% in October. title: MU, TSM Stocks Dip Overnight As Samsung Forecasts Record $80B Operating Profit In Q3 - Stocktwits
content: Samsung Electronics’ record third-quarter forecasts weighed on shares of competitors Micron Technology (MU) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing early Thursday, even as TSMC posted healthy sales growth for September. Samsung projected its quarterly operating profit for July through September would top 100 trillion won, a ​world first for a technology company. The company said operating profit is likely to be 107.4 trillion won, equivalent to $80.18 billion. Samsung will issue its full results on October 29. Close on the heels of Samsung’s report, TSMC said its September sales rose 54.6%, taking third-quarter sales 50% higher to 1.49 trillion won. MU slipped nearly 1% in overnight trading ahead of Thursday, while U.S.-listed shares of TSMC dipped 0.3%. Samsung’s stock ended 2.4% lower in Seoul. Samsung competes with Micron in memory chips such as DRAM and HBM, while it competes with TSMC in semiconductor foundry services. Samsung’s operating profit forecast topped analysts' estimate of 106.1 trillion won, according to LSEG SmartEstimate cited by Reuters, and would mark Samsung’s fourth consecutive quarter of record operating profit. It also exceeds the roughly 89 trillion won record set in the second quarter. Revenue is expected to more than double year over year to a record 195 trillion won, Samsung said, although the figure fell short of a FactSet consensus estimate of 206.8 trillion won cited by The Wall Street Journal. The semiconductor business is expected to have driven the bulk of Samsung’s earnings growth, as surging AI infrastructure spending fuels demand for both conventional and high-bandwidth memory. Samsung and Micron have warned that tight memory supply could persist through 2028, while Samsung expects shortages to worsen next year. Samsung’s shares have slumped more than 25% from a ​record high in June amid concerns about the durability of the AI boom. TSMC’s Q3 revenue beat analysts’ expectations of $1.46 trillion, according to an LSEG SmartEstimate. The strong performance further indicates the strength of AI-related semiconductor demand. The Taiwanese chipmaker will report its full third-quarter results ​next Thursday, ⁠when it will also update its outlook and plans for the current quarter and the rest of the year. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘bearish’ for both MU and TSM as of early Thursday. “$TSM Should we worry about September revenue being down 0.6% from August?” a trader questioned. (NIO) are poised to end a five-week losing streak as Onvo crosses 200,000 cumulative deliveries and battery swaps hit a fresh holiday record, giving retail bulls fresh milestones to weigh against persistent sales pressure. Nio’s U.S.-listed shares rose 2% in the previous session to $3.54, and are up 5% through Wednesday. Onvo marked its 200,000th delivery on Thursday, handing over a flagship L90 SUV to the family of Chinese television host Geng Chenchen. The family-focused brand reached the milestone roughly two years after L60 deliveries began in September 2024. Its lineup now includes three electric SUVs: the L60, L80 and L90, CnEVPost noted. Onvo ended September with 198,760 cumulative deliveries, implying it delivered another 1,240 vehicles this month. China’s Oct.1-Oct.7 National Day holiday typically slows automotive production and handovers. The cumulative milestone comes against weaker recent sales. Onvo delivered 8,763 vehicles in September, down 43% from a year earlier and 0.5% from August, marking its fourth consecutive monthly decline. Third-quarter deliveries fell 26% from a year ago to 27,728. Deliveries across the first nine months were nearly flat at 70,191, up just 1%. While Onvo works to rebuild sales momentum, Nio’s swapping network saw record holiday demand. The company completed 183,664 battery swaps on Monday, up from 183,469 on Oct. 1. The new peak was 4.4% above February’s Lunar New Year record and 7.7% above the May 1 total, EV reported. Across the network, that equates to roughly one completed swap every 0.47 seconds. “For long-distance driving, swapping is the first choice,” Nio said on Weibo. The holiday peaks underscore the role of highway infrastructure for drivers making longer journeys. Nio said its highway swapping network connects more than 550 cities and allows drivers to reach every provincial-level region of mainland China using swap stations. Nio’s network map showed 4,165 swap stations in China on Wednesday, including 1,072 on highways. It also listed 5,376 charging stations with 31,005 charging piles. Cumulative swaps exceeded 127 million, while charging sessions passed 100 million. Drivers of other brands accounted for 86.7% of the energy delivered by Nio’s own chargers, according to the map. The company still faces a substantial construction push to meet its target of adding 1,000 swap stations this year. With 489 added so far, another 511 would need to open before year-end, requiring 5.9 openings a day. Partner funding could support that expansion. Geely Holding Group agreed last month to acquire a 30% stake in Nio Power in a deal valuing the charging and swapping business at approximately 16 billion yuan, or $2.4 billion. Nio’s longer-term target is 10,000 swap stations by 2030. Battery swapping is also part of Onvo’s pitch to family buyers. Its vehicles share Nio’s charging, swapping and service infrastructure, giving the brand access to the expanding network. Onvo refreshed the L90 in April, launched the five-seat L80 in May and updated the entry-level L60 in June. Selected variants feature Nio’s in-house Shenji NX9031 driver-assistance chip, LiDAR and the Nio World Model system. The brand added new design packages for the L80 and L90 in September and said pn Thursday that it now operates 374 service centers across 213 Chinese cities. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) are tracking a second straight weekly gain as the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) outlined proposals that could expand satellite-to-smartphone services for SpaceX and rival Amazon, while Jeff Bezos floated an eventual Blue Origin IPO. SPCX stock rose 0.4% overnight heading into Thursday after falling 2.5% on Wednesday to $167.60. Shares are also up 5% for the week. The FCC said on Wednesday that it would vote Oct.29 on a proposal to auction 25 megahertz of “prime spectrum” to support direct-to-device services connecting satellites to smartphones. The agency also plans to vote on seeking public comment on making an additional 482 MHz available for supplemental coverage from space and modernizing rules governing direct-to-device services in licensed spectrum. The proposals could broaden opportunities for SpaceX and Amazon, which are expanding satellite networks to reach users beyond conventional wireless coverage. The votes would advance the regulatory process rather than immediately release all the proposed spectrum. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the measures aim to “end cell phone dead zones and provide service directly from next-gen satellite constellations to your smartphone.” The proposals came a day after the FCC Space Bureau approved SpaceX’s new 15,000-satellite direct-to-cell system, which will use spectrum purchased from EchoStar in a deal the agency cleared earlier this year. Amazon is building its own satellite-to-phone business. In July, it sought FCC approval for up to 5,105 satellites to connect users “unserved or underserved” by existing wireless providers. The following month, it agreed to acquire Globalstar for more than $11.5 billion to bolster its Leo satellite internet business. The FCC’s October meeting could mark another step toward opening more spectrum to both companies as they compete to connect smartphones from space. Bezos also opened the door Wednesday to an eventual Blue Origin listing, potentially giving investors another major space company to consider following SpaceX’s June IPO. “I think, someday, Blue Origin will have an IPO,” he told Fox News’ “Special Report with Bret Baier,” adding that it would be “several years from now.” Blue Origin recently raised $10 billion in its first outside funding round at a reported $140 billion valuation. Bezos said he had personally invested $28 billion since founding the company in 2000 and waited until its financial future became clearer before bringing in other investors. “I didn’t really want to take outside investors until I was sure that it would be a good investment for them,” he said. The company, separately owned from Amazon, has secured multibillion-dollar NASA and U.S. Space Force contracts, including work on the Artemis lunar program. Musk welcomed Bezos’ commitment, saying: “Bravo! I’m glad @JeffBezos cares so much about space.” Before any listing, Blue Origin aims to return New Glenn to flight after a May launch-pad explosion during a static-fire test disrupted its commercial-launch ambitions. “December of this year, we’re going to fly that vehicle again,” Bezos said. Wei explained that TSMC runs a sophisticated and disciplined capacity planning process, factoring in CSP CapEx, data center build-out, power supply, and other supply chain components. Based on its assessment, demand still exceeds supply, and TSMC is working hard to narrow the gap. CFO Wendell Huang added that demand is extremely robust with no sign of slowdown, and the AI accelerator CAGR will probably be higher than the previously guided mid- to high 50s percentage from 2024 to 2029. Q: Gokul Hariharan of JPMorgan asked whether wafer supply tightness in 2027 could be even greater than in 2026, and whether TSMC's wafer capacity growth could approach or exceed 10% in the next couple of years.A: C.C. Wei said demand is extremely robust and getting higher, with TSMC checking data center build-out and customer demand from multiple angles. The gap between demand and supply remains quite big, and TSMC is putting all its strength into increasing capacity. Wendell Huang added it is too early to discuss capacity increase percentages, but advanced nodes are the main driver of capacity growth. Q: Gokul Hariharan of JPMorgan also asked about TSMC's more aggressive overseas expansion, including potential new fab clusters in Texas and engagement with a customer's Terafab project.A: C.C. Wei confirmed TSMC is expanding in the US because most large customers are there and the US government is helpful. TSMC has evaluated locations outside Arizona, including Texas, and is in discussions with a customer about potentially utilizing Terafab capacity. He emphasized that any such fab must be run by TSMC, and more details will be shared once discussions conclude. Q: Krish Sankar of TD Cowen asked about a secondary wafer market where customers pass wafer allocation to others, and whether TSMC allows this practice.A: C.C. Wei stated this is not a new strategy and TSMC does not allow customers to sublet or auction off capacity. In certain cases, customers can collaborate through mask licensing agreements, but this is not common practice and the amount is very small. Q: Krish Sankar of TD Cowen also asked whether adopting High NA EUV later than competitors, around 2030, puts TSMC at a competitive disadvantage.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC always evaluates new tools for best technology, reasonable cost, and maturity. TSMC plans to use High NA in 2030 when it believes the tool will be mature and cost-effective, and is working with ASML on a 12-inch photomask by 2031. He emphasized TSMC remains confident it is still the best company to offer the most advanced technology to customers. Q: Charlie Chan of Morgan Stanley asked about an IDM customer spending aggressively on capacity and whether A14 could still be a bigger node than N2 despite potential insourcing.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC treats every customer fairly, whether IDM or fabless, and takes internal customer capacity into consideration. TSMC has seen more customer activity for A14 than for 2-nanometer so far and expects A14 to be a bigger node than N2. He declined to comment on specific customer outsourcing plans but guaranteed TSMC takes everything into consideration. Q: Charlie Chan of Morgan Stanley also asked about advanced packaging, including whether TSMC's SoW 3.5D can catch customers moving to larger reticle sizes like 14x, and whether TSMC would support customers if they cannot get sufficient capacity from a competitor's EMIB-T solution.A: C.C. Wei said TSMC's advanced packaging technology is very competitive, with the top priority being to help customers' products reach the market smoothly with best technology and enough capacity. TSMC is in real-world production of 5x reticle size with excellent yield, working on 9x and moving to 14x reticle size. CoWoS remains the number one choice for customers, and TSMC remains very competitive. Q: Sunny Lin of UBS asked how to think about CapEx beyond 2026, including whether CapEx could grow faster than or in line with sales, and whether tool price inflation is a meaningful variable for 2027 CapEx.A: Wendell Huang said it is too early to share CapEx numbers beyond this year, but TSMC has strong conviction in the AI megatrend, and CapEx from 2026 to 2028 is expected to be significantly higher than the past three years. Tool price inflation is real, but the majority of CapEx is related to long-term demand. He added that if TSMC does its job right, revenue growth will outpace CapEx growth. Q: Sunny Lin of UBS also asked about the wider 3% to 4% overseas margin dilution starting in 2027, and whether Arizona expansion is being accelerated.A: Wendell Huang said TSMC is doing everything it can to increase capacity and accelerating everywhere, including in the US. The 3 to 4 percentage point margin dilution from overseas fabs in the latter part of the five-year period remains the case. Q: Haas Liu of Bank of America asked about potential shifts in AI demand mix toward more efficient compute solutions, including agentic AI CPUs and networking switches, and the incremental opportunity for TSMC's manufacturing and packaging business.A: C.C. Wei said AI demand is extremely robust, whether from accelerators or CPUs, and TSMC has seen demand from agentic AI CPUs continue to increase. In TSMC's judgment, demand is still far above its ability to supply, and TSMC is working hard to narrow the gap. Q: Haas Liu of Bank of America also asked whether supporting both conventional power delivery and super power rail technology at future nodes makes the yield learning curve more challenging and impacts gross margins.A: C.C. Wei said the situation is different from previous years, with strong demand from both smartphone and AI HPC applications, and smaller die sizes and large accelerator die sizes happening at the same time. This is to TSMC's advantage because it has been prepared for this, results are excellent, and customers are very happy.
